title: Cardiac surgical outcomes and predictors of redo sternotomy in patients with Marfan syndrome: a retrospective multicentre cohort study

Abstract Background Marfan syndrome (MFS) is associated with progressive aortic and valvular disease requiring cardiac surgery, but contemporary data on repeat cardiac operations in adults remain limited. Methods We performed a retrospective multicentre cohort study of 783 adults with MFS evaluated across three Mayo Clinic sites. Cardiac operations, postoperative complications, echocardiographic findings and redo sternotomy events were identified by chart review. Multivariate logistic regression was used to evaluate factors associated with redo sternotomy. Results Overall, 454 patients (58.0%) underwent at least one cardiac operation, and 185 patients (23.6% of the total cohort; 41.0% of operated patients) required redo sternotomy. The most common procedures were aortic root intervention (53.4%), aortic valve intervention (39.6%), mitral valve intervention (16.1%) and tricuspid valve intervention (2.6%). Valvular abnormalities were frequent, including mitral regurgitation (51.5%), mitral valve prolapse (41.1%), tricuspid regurgitation (44.6%) and aortic regurgitation (28.5%). Major postoperative complications occurred in 15.3% of patients. On multivariate analysis, hypertension (OR 2.39, 95% CI 1.54 to 3.72), emergent initial operation (OR 3.38, 95% CI 1.97 to 5.80) and postoperative complications (OR 2.59, 95% CI 1.58 to 4.27) were independently associated with redo sternotomy, whereas repair extending beyond the aortic root was associated with lower odds (OR 0.39, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.53). Conclusion In this large multicentre cohort of adults with MFS, cardiac surgery was common, and redo sternotomy occurred frequently among operated patients. These findings provide a contemporary description of the long-term need for cardiac surgery in adults with MFS managed at tertiary referral centres. However, patients remain at risk for distal aortic progression and recurrent valvular pathology, often requiring additional surgical interventions. Despite this, large contemporary studies examining the cumulative burden of cardiac surgery and predictors of reoperation in adults with Marfan syndrome are limited. WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS This multicentre cohort study demonstrates that cardiac surgery is common in adults with Marfan syndrome, with a substantial proportion requiring redo sternotomy over time. It identifies hypertension, emergent initial surgery and postoperative complications as independent factors associated with redo sternotomy, while more extensive initial aortic repair is associated with lower odds of reoperation. These findings provide a contemporary, large-scale characterisation of surgical burden and associated factors in this population. HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY These findings highlight the importance of long-term surveillance and multidisciplinary management in patients with Marfan syndrome. Recognition of factors associated with redo sternotomy may help inform risk stratification, surgical planning and postoperative care. Future research should focus on prospective longitudinal data and strategies to reduce the need for repeat interventions. Introduction Marfan syndrome (MFS) is a systemic connective-tissue disorder caused by pathogenic variants in FBN1 , predisposing to progressive dilation of the aortic root, valvular dysfunction and life-threatening aortic dissection. 1 2 Advances in surgical and medical management have transformed survival, yet affected individuals continue to experience substantial cardiovascular morbidity and require repeated interventions throughout life. 3 4 Aortic root replacement remains the cornerstone of therapy, but the optimal timing, extent and long-term durability of these operations remain subjects of debate. 5 Historically, the introduction of elective root replacement and valve-sparing techniques markedly reduced mortality compared with emergent repair of acute dissection. 6 However, progressive distal aortic enlargement and valvular disease continue to drive the need for reintervention. 7 Recent series have shown that even after successful aortic root repair, patients with MFS frequently require additional operations for distal aneurysm formation, valve degeneration or postoperative complications. 3 Valvular involvement is also common in MFS and contributes meaningfully to long-term surgical morbidity. 8 Despite extensive literature on surgical techniques, large multicentre analyses examining the cardiac surgical burden and factors associated with reoperation in adults with MFS remain limited. Redo sternotomy may occur for heterogeneous indications, including progressive aortic disease, valvular pathology or complications related to prior surgery, and may serve as a clinically relevant marker of cumulative cardiac operative burden in this population. Accordingly, this study sought to (1) characterise the spectrum of cardiac surgical procedures performed in patients with MFS, (2) quantify postoperative complications and the occurrence of redo sternotomy as a marker of cumulative cardiac surgical burden and (3) identify clinical and procedural factors associated with redo sternotomy. By focusing on descriptive and associative analyses, this study aims to provide a contemporary framework for understanding long-term cardiac surgical outcomes in adults with MFS managed at tertiary referral centres. Methodology Study population This retrospective cohort study analysed patients diagnosed with MFS across all Mayo Clinic sites in Rochester, Arizona and Florida between 2012 and 2025. Patients were included based on follow-up within Mayo Clinic during this period, although some cardiovascular operations may have occurred earlier and were captured through detailed chart review. Patients were identified using International Classification of Diseases codes and confirmed through detailed manual chart review. Diagnostic confirmation was based on either genetic testing demonstrating a likely pathogenic or pathogenic FBN1 variant or phenotypic diagnosis established according to the revised Ghent criteria, including findings such as aortic root aneurysm or dissection, ectopia lentis, characteristic systemic features and/or a family history of genetically confirmed MFS. Our initial cohort included 1113 patients, which was refined to 783 after application of strict inclusion and exclusion criteria. Individuals younger than 18 years were excluded. Patient and public involvement Patients and members of the public were not involved in the design, conduct, reporting or dissemination plans of this research. Summary of cardiovascular interventions Data were extracted on all cardiac surgeries, including aortic root replacement, aortic valve repair or replacement (AVR), tricuspid valve repair or replacement (TV surgery), mitral valve repair or replacement (MV surgery) and closure of atrial or ventricular septal defects (ASD, VSD) or patent foramen ovale (PFO). The specific surgery type and corresponding dates were recorded to determine the prevalence of each intervention. For all patients who underwent AVR, MV surgery or TV surgery, further details were collected regarding the type of prosthetic valve (mechanical vs bioprosthetic), and the anticoagulation regimen initiated postoperatively. The analysis specifically focused on sternotomy-based cardiac and proximal thoracic aortic operations. Descending thoracic aortic procedures performed via thoracotomy and abdominal aortic procedures performed via laparotomy were not systematically included, as these fell outside the scope of the current study. Postoperative outcomes and complications An in-depth chart review was conducted to document clinically significant postoperative complications following cardiac surgery. Long-term follow-up identified patients who underwent redo sternotomy, with dates and operative indications abstracted from operative reports and clinical documentation. Cases in which either the initial or redo operation was performed for pectus repair were excluded to isolate cardiac and aortic indications. Echocardiographic assessment Echocardiographic studies were reviewed for all patients, including preoperative imaging and the most recent echocardiogram available during follow-up. These studies were used to assess valvular structure and function, including the presence and severity of mitral and tricuspid regurgitation, aortic valve dysfunction and mitral valve prolapse (MVP). The function and integrity of all prosthetic valves were also evaluated. Aortic assessment on transthoracic echocardiography was based on Echocardiography Information Management System using body surface area-adjusted, age-adjusted and sex-adjusted thresholds. An individual was classified as positive when the measured diameter at the mid-ascending aorta or sinus of Valsalva exceeded the expected threshold for that patient at the corresponding location. For other imaging modalities, aneurysm status was based on the interpreting report when the vessel was described as aneurysmal. Given the retrospective nature of the study, patients were considered positive if they had at least one documented imaging event above dilation or aneurysm threshold. Patients who underwent surgery were considered positive if aneurysmal disease had been documented before surgery. Study outcomes The primary outcomes were the prevalence of cardiac surgeries, major postoperative complications and redo sternotomy. The primary descriptive objectives were to characterise the spectrum of cardiac surgical procedures and postoperative complications, whereas the primary analytic outcome was redo sternotomy among patients who underwent at least one cardiac operation. Redo sternotomy was analysed among patients who underwent at least one cardiac operation, and operative indications were recorded. Secondary outcomes included echocardiographic characterisation of valvular abnormalities before and after surgery, identification of MVP and characterisation of valve type (mechanical vs bioprosthetic) among patients undergoing valve intervention. Statistical analysis Categorical variables were summarised using frequencies and percentages (n, %). Continuous variables were assessed for normality using the Shapiro-Wilk test and presented as mean±SD or median with IQR, as appropriate. Variables of interest were subsequently included in multivariate logistic regression models to identify independent associations. Multivariable logistic regression was used to evaluate factors associated with the occurrence of redo sternotomy as a clinically relevant outcome. Survival analysis was not performed because detailed and reliable time-to-event data, particularly for surgeries performed many years prior, were not consistently available across the retrospective cohort, precluding robust time-to-event modelling. All analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics, and p value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results Study population The study included a total of 783 patients diagnosed with MFS. Among them, 340 (43.4%) were women and 443 (56.6%) were men. The median age was 53 years (IQR 24). A total of 353 patients (45.1%) had a genetically confirmed diagnosis, while the remainder were diagnosed phenotypically. Most patients were white (680, 86.8%). The median left ventricular ejection fraction was 60% (IQR 8%). Hypertension was present in 348 patients (44.4%), diabetes mellitus in 46 (5.9%), chronic kidney disease in 91 (11.6%), migraine in 116 (14.8%) and a history of stroke or transient ischaemic attack in 58 (7.4%). Heart failure was reported in 136 (17.4%) and obesity in 100 (12.8%). Table 1 presents the basic characteristics of the study population, and key findings are summarised in figure 1 . Valvular abnormalities prior to surgical interventions Of the 783 patients, 635 (81.1%) had an ascending aortic aneurysm and 179 (22.9%) had an abdominal aortic aneurysm. A total of 204 (26.0%) presented with aortic dissection (type A, 14.6%; type B, 14.7%), with some having both types. Mitral regurgitation (MR) was present in 403 patients (51.5%), including 177 (22.6%) with moderate or greater MR (92 (11.8%) severe, 85 (10.9%) moderate). MVP was identified in 322 (41.1%). Tricuspid regurgitation (TR) occurred in 349 (44.6%) patients, including 128 (16.3%) with moderate or greater TR (20 (2.6%) severe, 108 (13.8%) moderate). 26 patients (3.3%) had a bicuspid aortic valve, and 13 (1.7%) had aortic stenosis. Aortic regurgitation (AR) was present in 223 (28.5%) patients, including 145 (18.5%) with moderate or greater AR (91 (11.6%) severe, 54 (6.9%) moderate). A summary of valvular abnormalities is presented in table 2 . Prevalence of surgical interventions A total of 454 patients (58.0%) underwent at least one surgical intervention, with some patients undergoing multiple procedures during a single operation. Aortic root intervention, with or without concomitant ascending aortic or arch involvement, was performed in 418 patients (53.4%). Aortic valve surgery was performed in 310 patients (39.6%), including mechanical valve implantation in 262 (33.5%), bioprosthetic valve implantation in 31 (4.0%) and aortic valve repair in 17 (2.2%). Mitral valve intervention was performed in 126 patients (16.1%), comprising mechanical valve implantation in 55 (7.0%), bioprosthetic valve implantation in 5 (0.6%) and mitral valve repair in 66 (8.4%). Tricuspid valve intervention was performed in 20 patients (2.6%), including mechanical valve implantation in 5 (0.6%) and tricuspid valve repair in 15 (1.9%). Additionally, 9 patients (1.1%) underwent ASD/VSD closure and 26 (3.3%) underwent PFO closure. A summary of cardiac surgical interventions is presented in table 3 . Complications A total of 120 patients (15.3%) experienced at least one postoperative complication, including 99 (12.6%) after the initial surgery and 21 (2.7%) following redo sternotomy. The most common events were infection (26 patients, 3.3%), respiratory failure requiring intubation or tracheostomy (21, 2.7%), haemodynamic instability or bleeding requiring transfusion or vasopressors (22, 2.8%) and effusion or tamponade requiring drainage (27, 3.4%). Neurologic events occurred in 17 patients (2.2%) (including 11 stroke, 3 seizure, 2 spinal cord ischaemia and 1 significant critical illness neuropathy), vascular in 13 (1.7%) and other complications in 30 (3.8%), including heart failure, pulmonary embolism, limb ischaemia, wound dehiscence or sternal nonunion. Patients could experience more than one complication type. Redo sternotomy A total of 185 patients (41.0% of those who underwent at least one surgical procedure) required redo sternotomy. The primary indication was progressive aortic aneurysm enlargement necessitating reintervention, including enlargement of the ascending aorta, in 110 patients (59.5% of those undergoing redo sternotomy). Other indications included aortic dissection in 32 patients (17.3%) and isolated valve replacement in 35 patients (18.9%). The remaining 8 patients (4.3%) underwent redo sternotomy for other cardiac indications, including tricuspid valve replacement, postoperative complications or coronary artery bypass grafting. The mean interval from the initial surgery to redo sternotomy was 8.48 years (SD 8.45). Predictors of redo sternotomy On univariate logistic regression, age ≥40 years was associated with higher redo risk (86.5% vs 79.2%, OR=1.68, 95% CI 1.01 to 2.81, p=0.047), while gender was not (p=0.866). Hypertension was present in 64.9% of redo cases versus 48.3% of non-redo cases (OR=1.97, 95% CI 1.34 to 2.90, p<0.001). Emergent initial operation was associated with a more than threefold increased risk (OR=3.25, 95% CI 1.99 to 5.30, p<0.001). Extent of surgery was significant: procedures extending beyond the aortic root were associated with a lower likelihood of redo (OR=0.45, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.59, p<0.001). Experiencing a complication after the first surgery also doubled redo risk (OR=2.54, 95% CI 1.61 to 4.00, p<0.001). On multivariate analysis, hypertension (OR=2.39, 95% CI 1.54 to 3.72, p<0.001), emergent initial operation (OR=3.38, 95% CI 1.97 to 5.80, p<0.001) and postoperative complication (OR=2.59, 95% CI 1.58 to 4.27, p<0.001) independently predicted redo sternotomy, while surgery extending beyond the aortic root remained protective (OR=0.39, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.53, p<0.001). Age ≥40 years (OR=1.38, 95% CI 0.78 to 2.44, p=0.265) and valve-sparing surgery (OR=0.83, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.29, p=0.409) were not independently associated with redo sternotomy after adjustment. Discussion This multicentre study of 783 adults with MFS provides one of the largest contemporary descriptions of the long-term need for cardiac surgery and the factors linked to repeat sternotomy. More than half of patients underwent at least one cardiac operation, underscoring the substantial lifetime cardiac surgical burden associated with MFS. Valvular disease was highly prevalent, with mitral regurgitation present in over half of patients and MVP in more than 40%, consistent with prior reports of diffuse valvular involvement in MFS. 8 Redo sternotomy occurred in a substantial proportion of operated patients, reflecting the progressive and systemic nature of disease rather than isolated failure of their initial operation. The mechanisms underlying these findings are consistent with known biology of MFS. FBN1 mutations create protein that disrupt microfibril architecture and alter transforming growth factor-β signalling, weakening the integrity of the aortic wall and the connective tissue support of cardiac valves. 1 2 9 Although root replacement reduces the risk of catastrophic proximal aortic events, it does not eliminate the risk of later distal aortic degeneration or progressive valvular disease. 3 5 Data from the International Registry of Aortic Dissection and other longitudinal series demonstrate that distal aortic progression following root replacement remains common in this population. 7 In this context, redo sternotomy is best understood as an outcome that can arise for several different reasons, including progressive aortic disease, worsening valvular pathology and postoperative sequelae, and therefore reflects the long-term need for additional cardiac surgery rather than failure of any single operative strategy. At the same time, it should be interpreted within the scope of this study, which focused on sternotomy-based cardiac and proximal thoracic aortic procedures rather than all later aortic reinterventions. Hypertension was independently associated with redo sternotomy in multivariate analysis. Although causality cannot be inferred from this retrospective design, this association may reflect increased haemodynamic stress imposed on structurally vulnerable aortic and valvular tissue, potentially accelerating disease progression or complicating postoperative courses. Emergent initial operations were also strongly associated with redo sternotomy, a finding consistent with historical surgical experience demonstrating more complex operative trajectories following acute dissection compared with elective repair. 6 Patients who first come to surgery emergently often require more limited or staged repair under urgent conditions, which may leave residual disease that later leads to another operation. Notably, surgical extent beyond the aortic root was associated with lower odds of redo sternotomy. This observation likely reflects differences in disease distribution, operative selection and initial surgical strategy rather than a causal protective effect of more extensive repair. Patients undergoing broader repair at their first operation may have had more complete treatment of disease segments or closer longitudinal surveillance, both of which could influence subsequent reintervention rates. Importantly, valve-sparing approaches were not independently associated with redo sternotomy after adjustment, supporting prior literature demonstrating their durability when performed in appropriately selected patients. 4 Postoperative complications following the initial operation were also independently associated with redo sternotomy. This finding aligns with prior observations in congenital and connective-tissue disease cohorts, in which early postoperative morbidity is linked to more complex long-term surgical courses. 10 12 While redo sternotomy may occasionally be required to manage postoperative complications, these adverse events may also serve as markers of tissue fragility, operative complexity or physiologic vulnerability that predispose patients to additional surgery over time. From a clinical perspective, these findings highlight the substantial lifetime surgical burden experienced by adults with MFS and underscore the need for coordinated, longitudinal care. The associations identified in this study should be interpreted as descriptive rather than prescriptive and do not establish causality or optimal management strategies. They should also be viewed in the context of a time-dependent outcome that could not be fully analysed with survival modelling because standardised time-to-event data were not consistently available across this retrospective cohort. Taken together, these findings provide a contemporary framework for understanding the factors linked to redo sternotomy in a large multicentre tertiary referral cohort. Limitations This study has several limitations. Its retrospective design introduces potential selection and ascertainment bias, and the cohort reflects patients managed at tertiary referral centres, which may limit generalisability to broader Marfan populations. Although diagnoses were confirmed using genetic or phenotypic criteria, some degree of misclassification remains possible, particularly among phenotypically diagnosed individuals. Detailed operative variables, including graft materials, suture type and specific surgical techniques, were not uniformly available. In addition, this study focused on sternotomy-based cardiac and proximal thoracic aortic procedures and therefore did not systematically capture later descending thoracic or thoracoabdominal reinterventions performed through thoracotomy or laparotomy. Follow-up duration and imaging intervals varied, and standardised time-to-event analyses could not be performed because reliable operative timing and longitudinal follow-up data were not consistently available across the cohort. Patients with diagnosed hypertension could not be subdivided into controlled versus uncontrolled blood pressure, limiting assessment of the impact of blood pressure control on outcomes. The exclusion of patients younger than 18 years also means that early cardiovascular operations in paediatric patients with MFS were not captured. Finally, genotype-outcome associations and treatment effects could not be evaluated. Conclusion In a large multicentre cohort of adults with MFS, cardiac surgery was common and redo sternotomy occurred frequently among operated patients. Hypertension, emergent initial surgery and postoperative complications were associated with redo sternotomy, while more extensive repair beyond the aortic root was associated with lower odds of needing another sternotomy. Rather than pointing to failure of a single operation, redo sternotomy appears to reflect the ongoing need for additional cardiac surgery over time in a population with progressive aortic and valvular disease. These findings provide a contemporary descriptive assessment of the long-term need for repeat cardiac surgery in MFS and highlight clinical and procedural factors associated with a more complex later surgical course.
